newsitem.title: USA: Justice Department to push overturn of Prop 209.
newsitem.headline: Justice Department to push overturn of Prop 209.

text.p: The Justice Department has concluded that a California initiative outlawing affirmative action, Proposition 209, is unconstitutional and will back legal action to overturn it, the White House said on Friday.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said President Bill Clinton, who campaigned against the initiative in the Nov. 5 election, fully supported the move.

"Rather than remedying what's wrong with the affirmative action programmes that exist, (Proposition 209) has the effect of abolishing affirmative action," McCurry said. "The president believes that we need to continue to have that as a tool to remedy discrimination in our society."
In response, California Gov. Pete Wilson sent Clinton a letter stating his concerns about the administration's intervention in the Proposition 209 case.
"Unless you reconsider, your administration will now have the distinction of making a legal challenge that is absolutely Orwellian," Wilson, a Republican, said in the letter.
State Attorney General Dan Lungren, who is leading the defence of Proposition 209, said separately that the state was prepared to "battle" Clinton over the initiative.
Attorneys seeking to block the proposition lauded Clinton's support, saying it would significantly bolster their case.
"It's a major development," said Mark Rosenbaum, legal director of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Southern California. "It adds a red, white and blue nail in Proposition 209's coffin."

Proposition 209, the first initiative of its kind passed by any state, would bar preferential treatment based on race or sex in public employment, education and contracting. It was approved last month by a margin of 54 percent to 46 percent.

Implementation of the initiative is on hold, however. A federal judge in San Francisco earlier this week extended until Dec. 23 a temporary restraining order that is keeping California officials from rolling back affirmative action programmes.

The judge extended the temporary restraining order after hearing oral arguments earlier this week on whether to grant a preliminary injunction that would freeze Proposition 209 until a trial can be held on the measure's constitutionality.
The judge was expected to rule on the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction later Friday or Monday.

McCurry said the Justice Department would intervene in the case as a plaintiff rather than as a friend of the court. But officials at the department said the form of its intervention had not been decided.
Asked how the Clinton administration justified its effort to overrule California voters, McCurry said: "There's always strong preference that goes to the will of the people.
"However, if significant overriding constitutional concern presents itself, the president as the nation's chief constitutional officer has to act to defend the Constitution," he said.
Ward Connerly, a black California businessman who led the campaign for the initiative, blasted Clinton's decision, accusing him of caving into the "radical left."

"By joining the lawsuit against Proposition 209, President Clinton has betrayed his commitment to centrist politics," Connerly said. "He recently said he wanted to forge a coalition of the centre, yet by this action he joins the radical left."
